The Iiwi (Drepanis coccinea) is an iconic Hawaiian honeycreeper whose life history is closely tied to the archipelago's montane cloud forests. A newly hatched nestling emerges at a remarkably small mass of just 2.5 grams [Ww0 = 2.5 grams], reflecting the altricial state typical of many passerines. Incubation of the egg at 31 °C [T = 31 °C] yields a relatively brief developmental period, with hatching occurring after just 14 days [ab = 14 days]. This short incubation is likely an adaptation to the cool but stable microclimate of the nest cavity, where thermoregulatory demands on the brooding adult are significant. Upon hatching, the altricial nestling is entirely dependent on parental provisioning for warmth and nutrition, initiating a period of rapid mass gain that will ultimately lead to a body size several times greater than its birth weight.

Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in this species, a pattern often linked to differences in foraging ecology and parental investment. Females typically reach an ultimate wet weight of 16.7 grams [Wwi = 16.7 grams], a value that reflects the energetic constraints of egg production and brooding. Males, by contrast, attain a larger ultimate wet weight of 19.9 grams [Wwi = 19.9 grams], a size advantage that may enhance competitive ability in territorial disputes over high-quality nectar resources. These mass differences are consistent with the broader pattern observed across the Drepanidinae, where male-biased size dimorphism is common among nectarivorous forms that defend floral resources. The physiological cost of maintaining this larger body is reflected in the species' metabolic rate, measured under controlled conditions.

Basal metabolic rate in the Iiwi has been quantified through respirometry trials conducted at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a temperature that approximates the thermoneutral zone for this species. Under these conditions, the maximum basal metabolic rate was recorded at 62.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 62.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This value is modest relative to other passerines of comparable mass, suggesting an energy-conserving strategy typical of island endemics that have evolved in the absence of intense competition and high predation risk. The relatively low metabolic demand may also reflect dietary specialization on dilute nectar, which imposes constraints on energy acquisition rates. This energetic profile has implications for the timing of key life history events, which are also sensitive to thermal conditions.

This low fecundity, combined with a late age at first reproduction and a relatively long lifespan, positions the Iiwi as a classic slow life-history strategist among passerines, making its populations particularly vulnerable to environmental perturbations that affect adult survivorship.
